statement: Let $f$ be a continuous function on the unit circle. Then there is a unique function $g$ in the [Hardy space](c:hardy-space) $H^\infty$ with $\|f-g\|_\infty=\operatorname{dist}(f,H^\infty)$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is continuous on the unit circle.
The approximants range over the bounded analytic functions $H^\infty$ on the disc, with boundary values on the circle.

conclusion: A [best approximation](c:best-approximation) of $f$ in $H^\infty$ exists and is unique.

proofs.name: Duality and extremal functions
proofs.slogan: Find a best approximant by weak-star compactness, describe it by duality, and show two best approximants agree.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem as an outline of the published proof. Existence is classical; uniqueness for continuous $f$ is the deep part.

roles.why: Continuity of $f$ makes the error $f-g$ continuous, so its modulus has good boundary behavior.
The class $H^\infty$ is weak-star closed, which gives existence and the annihilator in $L^1$.

steps.slogan: Take a minimizing sequence and extract a weak-star limit in $H^\infty$.
steps.detail: The unit ball of $H^\infty$ is weak-star compact and the norm is weak-star lower semicontinuous. A minimizing sequence has a limit $g$ that reaches the distance.

steps.slogan: Describe the distance by duality with the annihilator of $H^\infty$ in $L^1$.
steps.detail: The Hahn-Banach theorem gives $\operatorname{dist}(f,H^\infty)=\sup |\int f h\,d\theta|$ over $h$ in the annihilator of $H^\infty$ with $\|h\|_1\le 1$. A best approximant makes this supremum sharp.

steps.slogan: Show that the error of a best approximant has constant modulus.
steps.detail: For continuous $f$ the extremal functional gives $f-g=d\,u$ with $|u|=1$ almost everywhere, where $d$ is the distance. The cited paper works this out through the factorization of the extremal function in $H^1$.

steps.slogan: Compare two best approximants and show that they coincide.
steps.detail: If $g_1,g_2$ are best, so is their average, and the errors have equal constant modulus. The cited paper shows that the averaged error then forces $g_1=g_2$, using the structure of the unimodular error.

concepts.c:hardy-space: The approximating class $H^\infty$ is the Hardy space of bounded analytic functions.
concepts.c:best-approximation: The theorem asserts existence and uniqueness of the nearest point of $H^\infty$.

source.ref: L. Carleson and S. Jacobs, Best uniform approximation by analytic functions, Arkiv for Matematik 10 (1972), 219-229.
source.note: The paper proves uniqueness of the best uniform approximation of a continuous function by $H^\infty$; the outline follows its duality approach.

statement: Let $X$ be a smooth projective complex [algebraic surface](c:algebraic-surface). Let $\omega_1,\omega_2$ be linearly independent [holomorphic 1-forms](c:holomorphic-1-form) with $\omega_1\wedge\omega_2=0$. Then there is a [fibration](c:fibration) $f\colon X\to C$ onto a smooth curve of genus at least 2 with $\omega_i=f^*\eta_i$ for holomorphic 1-forms $\eta_i$ on $C$.

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a smooth projective complex surface.
$\omega_1,\omega_2$ are linearly independent holomorphic 1-forms on $X$.
The wedge product $\omega_1\wedge\omega_2$ is zero.

conclusion: A fibration with connected fibres onto a curve of genus $g\ge 2$ exists and both forms are pullbacks from the curve.

proofs.name: Ratio of the forms as a fibration
proofs.slogan: Use the ratio of the two forms as a rational map, resolve it, and read the forms on the base curve.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Surface forms are closed because $X$ is compact K\u00e4hler.

roles.why: Projectivity makes holomorphic forms closed and allows resolution of the rational map.
Independence makes the ratio $\varphi=\omega_1/\omega_2$ nonconstant.
The zero wedge product says that $\omega_1,\omega_2$ are proportional at every point.

steps.slogan: Form the meromorphic ratio $\varphi=\omega_1/\omega_2$.
steps.detail: The wedge product vanishes, so at each point the two forms are proportional and $\omega_1=\varphi\,\omega_2$ for a meromorphic function $\varphi$. It is nonconstant because the forms are independent.

steps.slogan: Show that $d\varphi\wedge\omega_2=0$ using closedness.
steps.detail: A holomorphic form on a compact K\u00e4hler manifold is closed. Then $0=d\omega_1=d\varphi\wedge\omega_2$, so $d\varphi$ is proportional to $\omega_2$ and $\varphi$ is constant along the leaves of $\ker\omega_2$.

steps.slogan: Resolve $\varphi$ and take the Stein factorization to a curve $C$.
steps.detail: Blow up the indeterminacy points of $\varphi\colon X\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}^1$ and factor the resulting map as a map with connected fibres $X'\to C$ followed by a finite map. The fibres lie in the leaves of $\ker\omega_2$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\omega_1,\omega_2$ are pullbacks of forms on $C$.
steps.detail: Both forms vanish on the fibres, so each equals $f^*\eta_i$ for a meromorphic form $\eta_i$ on $C$. The pullback is holomorphic, so $\eta_i$ is holomorphic. The forms $\eta_1,\eta_2$ are independent.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $C$ has genus at least 2 and that $f$ is defined on $X$.
steps.detail: A curve with two independent holomorphic 1-forms has $g\ge2$. Exceptional curves of the blow-up are rational, so they map to points of $C$ and $f$ descends to $X$.

concepts.c:algebraic-surface: The proof resolves a rational map on the surface by blow-ups.
concepts.c:holomorphic-1-form: The two forms give the ratio and descend to the curve.
concepts.c:fibration: The ratio of the forms produces the fibration.

source.note: The proof of Castelnuovo-de Franchis in A. Beauville, Complex Algebraic Surfaces, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press 1996, chapter X.

statement: Let $K$ be a complete discretely valued field with perfect residue field and $L/K$ a finite abelian Galois extension with group $G$. If $v$ is a jump of the [upper numbering](c:upper-numbering) filtration $G^v$ of the [ramification groups](c:ramification-group), then $v$ is an integer.

hypotheses.text: $K$ is a complete discretely valued field with perfect residue field.
$L/K$ is a finite Galois extension with abelian group $G$.

conclusion: Every jump of the upper numbering filtration of $G$ is a nonnegative integer.

proofs.name: Lower jumps of an abelian group
proofs.slogan: Pass to a cyclic quotient and show that the lower jumps differ by multiples of an index, so the upper jumps are integers.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem as an outline of the published proof; the jump at $-1$ in the unramified part is excluded.

roles.why: The Herbrand functions and ramification groups need a complete discrete valuation with perfect residue field.
Commutativity of $G$ forces the divisibility between consecutive lower jumps.

steps.slogan: Reduce to a cyclic quotient that keeps the jump.
steps.detail: Upper numbering passes to quotients. A character of $G$ trivial on $G^{v+\epsilon}$ and nontrivial on $G^v$ gives a cyclic quotient with a jump at $v$.

steps.slogan: Write the upper jump with the Herbrand function of the lower jumps.
steps.detail: The upper jump is $v=\varphi(u)=\frac{1}{|G_0|}\sum_{i=1}^{u}|G_i|$ for a lower jump $u$. So integrality of $v$ is a divisibility statement about the orders $|G_i|$.

steps.slogan: Show that consecutive lower jumps differ by multiples of the index.
steps.detail: For $s\in G_i$ and $t\in G_j$ the commutator estimate of ramification groups and the injections $G_i/G_{i+1}\hookrightarrow U^i_L/U_L^{i+1}$ give, for abelian $G$, that $u_{k+1}-u_k$ is divisible by $[G_0:G_{u_k}]$. Serre proves this in Local Fields.

steps.slogan: Sum the Herbrand formula and read off an integer.
steps.detail: The divisibility turns each increment of $\varphi$ between lower jumps into an integer. By induction on the jumps, every upper jump $\varphi(u_k)$ is an integer.

concepts.c:upper-numbering: The theorem is about jumps of the upper numbering filtration.
concepts.c:ramification-group: The lower groups and their orders define the Herbrand function.
concepts.c:abelian-extension: Commutativity gives the divisibility between consecutive lower jumps.

source.ref: J.-P. Serre, Local Fields, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 67, Springer, 1979, chapter V, section 7.
source.note: Serre proves the Hasse-Arf theorem there; the outline follows his reduction and divisibility argument.

statement: Let $X$ be a complex projective manifold and $L$ a [semi-ample](c:semi-ample-sheaf) invertible sheaf with [Iitaka dimension](c:iitaka-dimension) at least 2. Then $H^i(X,L^{-1})=0$ for $i=0,1$.

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a complex projective manifold.
The invertible sheaf $L$ is semi-ample.
The Iitaka dimension of $L$ is at least 2.

proofs.name: Semi-ample morphism and cyclic cover
proofs.slogan: Use the morphism of a semi-ample power, cut by a smooth connected divisor, and compare with a cyclic cover.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem as an outline of Mumford's proof; the case $i=0$ is elementary and $i=1$ rests on the cited argument.

roles.why: Smoothness allows Bertini and Serre duality on $X$.
A power $L^m$ is generated by sections and defines a morphism.
The image of the morphism has dimension at least 2, so general divisors are connected.

steps.slogan: Replace $L$ by a base-point-free power and take its morphism.
steps.detail: Some power $L^m$ is generated by global sections. They define $f\colon X\to\mathbb{P}^N$ with $L^m=f^*\mathcal{O}(1)$, and the image has dimension equal to the Iitaka dimension.

steps.slogan: Show that the group $H^0(X,L^{-1})$ is zero.
steps.detail: Let $s\ne0$ be a section of $L^{-1}$ and $t\ne0$ a section of $L^m$. Then $s^mt$ is a nonzero constant, so $t$ has no zeros and $L^m$ is trivial. That contradicts the image of $f$ having dimension at least 2.

steps.slogan: Choose a smooth connected divisor in $|L^m|$.
steps.detail: Bertini gives a smooth general member $D$. The image of $f$ has dimension at least 2, so the preimage of a general hyperplane section is connected.

steps.slogan: Compare $H^1(X,L^{-1})$ with the cyclic cover branched along $D$.
steps.detail: The cyclic cover $\pi\colon Z\to X$ has $\pi_*\mathcal{O}_Z=\bigoplus_{k<m}L^{-k}$, so $H^1(X,L^{-1})$ is a summand of $H^1(Z,\mathcal{O}_Z)$. Mumford shows the summand vanishes through connectedness of $D$ and Kodaira-type vanishing.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $H^1(X,L^{-1})$ is zero.
steps.detail: The summand argument gives $H^1(X,L^{-1})=0$ for $L$ with Iitaka dimension at least 2.

concepts.c:semi-ample-sheaf: Semi-ampleness gives the morphism that defines the cover and the divisor.
concepts.c:iitaka-dimension: Dimension at least 2 makes general divisors connected.

source.ref: D. Mumford, Pathologies III, American Journal of Mathematics 89 (1967), 94-104.
source.note: Mumford proves the vanishing there; the outline gives the main ingredients, with Kodaira vanishing as the prerequisite.

statement: Let $X$ be a smooth projective complex surface and $L$ a [nef](c:nef-line-bundle) line bundle with $L^2>0$. Then $H^0(X,L^{-1})=H^1(X,L^{-1})=0$.

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a smooth projective complex surface.
The line bundle $L$ is nef.
The self-intersection $L^2$ is positive.

conclusion: The first two cohomology groups of $L^{-1}$ vanish.

proofs.name: Effective divisor and Kodaira vanishing
proofs.slogan: Write a power of $L$ as an effective divisor and prove vanishing for the dual by the exact sequence and Kodaira.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for surfaces as an outline of Ramanujam's proof; the Kawamata-Viehweg theorem is the general form.

roles.why: On a surface, Riemann-Roch and Serre duality control $h^0$ and $H^1$.
Nefness keeps $L\cdot C\ge0$ on every curve $C$, used in the divisor step.
Positive $L^2$ makes $h^0(L^m)$ grow like $m^2$, so a power is effective.

steps.slogan: Show that some power of $L$ has a nonzero section.
steps.detail: Riemann-Roch gives $\chi(L^m)=\tfrac12 m^2L^2+O(m)$, which is positive for large $m$. Also $h^2(L^m)=h^0(K-L^m)=0$ for large $m$, because $L^m\cdot H>K\cdot H$ for an ample $H$. So $h^0(L^m)>0$.

steps.slogan: Choose an effective divisor $D$ with $\mathcal{O}(D)=L^m$ and study its components.
steps.detail: Nefness gives $D\cdot C\ge0$ for components $C$ of $D$. Ramanujam studies such divisors through connectedness: numerically connected divisors have $h^0(\mathcal{O}_D)=1$.

steps.slogan: Pass to $H^1(K_X\otimes L)$ by Serre duality.
steps.detail: Serre duality gives $H^1(X,L^{-1})\cong H^1(X,K_X\otimes L)^\vee$. The aim is to show this group is zero.

steps.slogan: Use the exact sequence of $D$ to reduce to the case of Kodaira vanishing.
steps.detail: The sequence $0\to L^{-m}\to\mathcal{O}_X\to\mathcal{O}_D\to0$ and its long exact sequence compare $H^1(L^{-m})$ with $H^1(\mathcal{O}_X)$ and $H^0(\mathcal{O}_D)$. Ramanujam closes the gap with Kodaira vanishing.

steps.slogan: Conclude $H^1(X,L^{-1})=0$, and $H^0(X,L^{-1})=0$ as before.
steps.detail: The comparison shows $H^1(L^{-1})=0$. A nonzero section $s$ of $L^{-1}$ gives the nonzero constant $s^m\cdot t_D$, so $D=0$ and $L^2=0$, which is false.

concepts.c:nef-line-bundle: Nefness replaces ampleness and gives non-negative degree on curves.

source.ref: C. P. Ramanujam, Remarks on the Kodaira vanishing theorem, Journal of the Indian Mathematical Society 36 (1972), 41-51 (with a correction in 38 (1974), 121-124).
source.note: Ramanujam proves the vanishing for nef and big line bundles on surfaces; the outline lists his ingredients.

statement: Let $g\ge1$ and $H(g)=\lfloor(7+\sqrt{1+48g})/2\rfloor$. The largest [chromatic number](c:chromatic-number) of a simple graph with a [graph embedding](c:graph-embedding) in the closed orientable surface $S_g$ of genus $g$ is $H(g)$.

hypotheses.text: The surface $S_g$ is closed and orientable with genus $g\ge1$.
The graphs are finite and simple.

conclusion: Every such graph is $H(g)$-colorable, and some such graph needs $H(g)$ colors.

proofs.name: Euler bound and complete graphs
proofs.slogan: Prove the upper bound by Euler's formula and degeneracy, and the lower bound by embedding the complete graph $K_{H(g)}$.
proofs.scope: Orientable surfaces of genus $g\ge1$; the sphere is the four color theorem. The lower bound rests on the cited genus formula for complete graphs.

roles.why: The genus enters the Euler count $V-E+F\ge2-2g$ and the embedding of $K_H$.
Simple graphs have faces of at least three edges, so $3F\le2E$.

steps.slogan: Bound the edges by the Euler characteristic.
steps.detail: An embedding has $V-E+F\ge 2-2g$ and $3F\le 2E$ for a simple graph with $V\ge3$. Hence $E\le 3(V-2+2g)$, and $V\ge H+1$ with minimum degree at least $H$ would give $(H-6)V\le 12(g-1)$.

steps.slogan: Show that a graph on more than $H$ vertices has a vertex of degree below $H$.
steps.detail: The definition of $H$ gives $(H-2)(H-3)>12g$. Then $(H-6)(H+1)\le12(g-1)$ fails, so a vertex of degree at most $H-1$ exists. Remove it, color by induction with $H$ colors, and give the vertex a free color.

steps.slogan: Quote the genus of the complete graph $K_n$.
steps.detail: Ringel and Youngs prove that $K_n$ embeds in $S_h$ with $h=\lceil (n-3)(n-4)/12\rceil$, by current graph constructions in twelve residue classes of $n$ modulo 12. The proof is the deep part.

steps.slogan: Embed $K_{H(g)}$ in $S_g$ by adding handles.
steps.detail: The definition of $H$ gives $(H-3)(H-4)\le 12g$, so $\lceil (H-3)(H-4)/12\rceil\le g$. Adding handles to the surface keeps an embedding, so $K_H$ embeds in $S_g$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two bounds to get the exact maximum.
steps.detail: The graph $K_{H(g)}$ embeds in $S_g$ and needs $H(g)$ colors. Every embeddable graph needs at most $H(g)$ colors.

concepts.c:chromatic-number: The theorem gives the exact maximum chromatic number on a surface.
concepts.c:graph-embedding: The graphs are embedded in the surface, which gives faces and Euler's count.
concepts.c:surface: The genus of the surface sets the Euler characteristic and the bound.

source.ref: G. Ringel and J. W. T. Youngs, Solution of the Heawood map-coloring problem, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA 60 (1968), 438-445.
source.note: The paper proves the genus of $K_n$ for the residue classes; Heawood's upper bound steps are written out here.

statement: Let $V$ be an [orthomodular space](c:orthomodular-space) over a division ring $K$ with an involution, with an infinite orthonormal set. Then $K$ is $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{C}$ or the quaternions, with the standard involution, and $V$ is a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) over $K$.

hypotheses.text: $V$ is an orthomodular space: every closed subspace $W$ satisfies $V=W\oplus W^\perp$.
$V$ has an infinite orthonormal set.
The scalars form a division ring with an involution.

conclusion: The scalar ring is $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{C}$ or $\mathbb{H}$ and $V$ is complete.

proofs.name: Orthonormal sequence forces order and completeness
proofs.slogan: Use the infinite orthonormal set to order the scalars, make them Archimedean and complete, and then complete the space.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem as an outline of Soler's proof; the finite-dimensional case has no analogue.

roles.why: Orthomodularity gives projections onto closed subspaces and the Fourier expansion.
The infinite orthonormal set supplies enough vectors to test sums and bounds of scalars.
The scalar division ring is shown to be an ordered, complete skew field.

steps.slogan: Use orthomodularity to project onto spans of orthonormal vectors.
steps.detail: For closed spans of orthonormal vectors, $V=W\oplus W^\perp$ gives orthogonal projections and Fourier coefficients. Bessel-type inequalities hold in the scalar order.

steps.slogan: Show that the involution is positive definite and orders the scalars.
steps.detail: The infinite orthonormal set gives sums $\sum a_i^*a_i$ that behave as in an inner product space. This makes $K$ formally real with the order $a^*a$ positive, which Soler proves.

steps.slogan: Show that the real part of $K$ is Archimedean and complete.
steps.detail: Bounds on Fourier coefficients and the existence of projections force every bounded increasing sequence of self-adjoint scalars to converge. So the center of the ordered ring is $\mathbb{R}$.

steps.slogan: Identify $K$ as a finite-dimensional division algebra over $\mathbb{R}$.
steps.detail: The scalar ring is a division algebra over $\mathbb{R}$ with positive involution and bounded dimension. Frobenius' classification gives $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{C}$ or $\mathbb{H}$.

steps.slogan: Show that $V$ is complete using orthomodularity.
steps.detail: A Cauchy sequence in $V$ yields coordinates that converge in $K$. Orthomodularity splits off the span of a limiting expansion, so the limit vector exists and $V$ is a Hilbert space.

concepts.c:orthomodular-space: Orthomodularity gives the projections that drive the whole proof.
concepts.c:hilbert-space: Completeness of the space is the final conclusion.
concepts.c:division-ring: The scalars are classified as $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{C}$ or $\mathbb{H}$.

source.ref: M. P. Soler, Characterization of Hilbert spaces by orthomodular spaces, Communications in Algebra 23 (1995), 219-243.
source.note: Soler's paper contains the proof; S. S. Holland, Orthomodularity in infinite dimensions, Bulletin of the AMS 32 (1995), 205-234, gives an exposition.

statement: The exit-path functor identifies the $\infty$-category of conically smooth [stratified spaces](c:stratified-space), enlarged to striation sheaves, with the $\infty$-category of $(\infty,1)$-categories. A space goes to its [exit path category](c:exit-path-category).

hypotheses.text: The objects are sheaves on conically smooth stratified spaces that satisfy descent.

conclusion: Exit paths give an equivalence between striation sheaves and $(\infty,1)$-categories.

proofs.name: Exit paths on basics and Yoneda extension
proofs.slogan: Compute exit paths on basic stratified pieces, extend by colimits to striation sheaves, and check that this is an equivalence.
proofs.scope: Outline of the published proof; the equivalence is for $\infty$-categories modulo the stated finiteness conventions of the paper.

roles.why: Basics are the stratified pieces whose exit paths are computed directly.

steps.slogan: Define basic stratified spaces and their exit-path categories.
steps.detail: A basic is a product of a Euclidean space and a cone on a link. Its exit-path $\infty$-category is computed from the link, which gives the generating objects.

steps.slogan: Show that exit paths are fully faithful on basics.
steps.detail: Maps between basics with their exit-path categories are compared through the link and the smooth structure. This proves that the functor is fully faithful on the generators.

steps.slogan: Extend the functor to striation sheaves by colimits.
steps.detail: Striation sheaves are sheaves on basics with descent. The Yoneda extension of exit paths gives a colimit-preserving functor from them to $(\infty,1)$-categories.

steps.slogan: Show that the extended functor is an equivalence.
steps.detail: An inverse sends an $\infty$-category $\mathcal{C}$ to the sheaf of functors from exit paths of basics to $\mathcal{C}$. Descent for this sheaf and the comparison of the two composites finish the proof.

concepts.c:stratified-space: Stratified spaces are the objects that generate the sheaf side.
concepts.c:exit-path-category: The exit-path category carries a space to an $\infty$-category.

source.ref: D. Ayala, J. Francis and N. Rozenblyum, A stratified homotopy hypothesis, Journal of the European Mathematical Society 21 (2019), 1071-1137.
source.note: The paper proves the equivalence; the outline lists the main steps without the technical detail of conically smooth structures.

statement: Let $A$ be a countable [admissible set](c:admissible-set) and $T$ a set of sentences of the [infinitary logic](c:infinitary-logic) $L_A$ that is $\Sigma_1$ on $A$. If every subset of $T$ that belongs to $A$ has a model, then $T$ has a model.

hypotheses.text: $A$ is a countable admissible set.
$T$ is a set of $L_A$ sentences that is $\Sigma_1$ on $A$.
Every subset of $T$ that is an element of $A$ has a model.

proofs.name: Henkin construction inside the admissible set
proofs.slogan: Show that a theory without models has a proof in $A$, and a proof in $A$ uses only an element of $A$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem as an outline of the published proof; ordinary compactness is the case of the hereditarily finite sets.

roles.why: Admissibility supplies $\Sigma$ recursion and reflection used to code proofs inside $A$.
The $\Sigma_1$ definition makes the set of consequences $\Sigma_1$ on $A$.
Models of the small subsets rule out a refutation lying in $A$.

steps.slogan: Code derivations of $L_A$ as elements of $A$ and show that derivability is $\Sigma_1$.
steps.detail: Barwise defines the proof system of $L_A$ with infinitary rules and codes proofs as sets. Admissibility makes the set of provable sentences of a $\Sigma_1$ theory $\Sigma_1$ on $A$.

steps.slogan: Run the Henkin construction on $L_A$ with new constants.
steps.detail: Add witnesses for existential sentences and decide each sentence in turn. If $T$ is consistent in $A$, this builds a complete Henkin theory and a countable model.

steps.slogan: Deduce the completeness theorem: consistency in $A$ gives a model.
steps.detail: The Henkin model satisfies $T$, so a $\Sigma_1$ theory with no model proves a contradiction by a proof in $A$ (Barwise completeness).

steps.slogan: Use $\Sigma$ reflection to put the proof inside a subset of $T$ in $A$.
steps.detail: A proof of a contradiction from $T$ is a set in $A$. It uses only a set $T_0\subseteq T$ that lies in $A$ by $\Sigma$ reflection. Then $T_0$ has no model.

steps.slogan: Contradict the hypothesis to get a model of $T$.
steps.detail: The set $T_0$ has a model by hypothesis, so it cannot prove a contradiction. So $T$ has a model.

concepts.c:admissible-set: Admissibility gives the recursion and reflection principles of the proof.
concepts.c:infinitary-logic: The logic $L_A$ is the infinitary language of the theorem.

source.ref: J. Barwise, Admissible Sets and Structures, Perspectives in Mathematical Logic, Springer, 1975, chapter III.
source.note: The book proves the completeness and compactness theorems for countable admissible fragments; the theorem was first proved in Barwise's 1967 thesis.

statement: Let $(M,\omega)$ be a [symplectic manifold](c:symplectic-manifold) of dimension $2n$ and $f_1,\dots,f_k$ smooth functions with pairwise zero [Poisson bracket](c:poisson-bracket) and independent differentials at $p$. Then there are Darboux coordinates $(q,y)$ near $p$ with $y_i=f_i$ for $i\le k$.

hypotheses.text: $(M,\omega)$ is a symplectic manifold of dimension $2n$.
The functions satisfy $\{f_i,f_j\}=0$ for all $i,j$.
The differentials $df_1,\dots,df_k$ are linearly independent at $p$.

conclusion: Darboux coordinates exist in which $f_1,\dots,f_k$ are $k$ of the momentum coordinates.

proofs.name: Induction by symplectic reduction
proofs.slogan: Find a conjugate function to $f_1$, reduce to a smaller symplectic manifold, and apply induction.
proofs.scope: Local statement near $p$, with $k\ge1$. The case $k=0$ is Darboux's theorem, which the induction uses.

roles.why: Nondegeneracy of $\omega$ makes the Hamiltonian fields independent and the reduction symplectic.
Zero brackets make the Hamiltonian fields commute and keep $f_j$ invariant under the flows.
Independence of the differentials gives independent Hamiltonian fields.

steps.slogan: Show that the Hamiltonian fields $X_{f_i}$ commute and are independent.
steps.detail: The identity $[X_f,X_g]=X_{\{f,g\}}$ gives $[X_{f_i},X_{f_j}]=0$. Nondegeneracy turns independent differentials into independent fields at $p$.

steps.slogan: Choose a function $g$ with $\{f_1,g\}=1$ and $\{f_j,g\}=0$ for $j\ge2$.
steps.detail: Commuting independent fields have common flow-box coordinates $(t_1,\dots,t_k,u)$ with $X_{f_i}=\partial_{t_i}$. Take $g=t_1$, so $\{f_i,g\}=X_{f_i}g=\delta_{i1}$.

steps.slogan: Reduce to the level set $N=\{f_1=c,\ g=d\}$, a symplectic manifold of dimension $2n-2$.
steps.detail: Since $\{f_1,g\}=1\ne0$, the form $\omega$ restricts nondegenerately to $N$. The flows of $X_{f_1}$ and $X_g$ commute, preserve each $f_j$, and identify a neighborhood of $p$ with $N\times\mathbb{R}^2$ symplectically.

steps.slogan: Apply the induction hypothesis to $f_2,\dots,f_k$ on $N$.
steps.detail: The restrictions $f_j|_N$ for $j\ge2$ commute and are independent, because $f_j$ is invariant under both flows. Induction gives Darboux coordinates on $N$ in which they are momenta. The case $k=0$ is Darboux's theorem.

steps.slogan: Combine the coordinates of $N$ with $(g,f_1)$ to get Darboux coordinates on $M$.
steps.detail: On $N\times\mathbb{R}^2$ the form is $\omega_N+dy_1\wedge dq_1$ with $y_1=f_1$ and $q_1=\pm g$. Together with the coordinates of $N$ these are Darboux coordinates in which $y_i=f_i$ for $i\le k$.

concepts.c:symplectic-manifold: The proof reduces the symplectic manifold to one of smaller dimension.
concepts.c:poisson-bracket: Zero brackets make the flows commute and keep $f_j$ invariant.

source.note: The standard induction proof by symplectic reduction, as in Libermann and Marle, Symplectic Geometry and Analytical Mechanics, chapter III.

statement: Let $F_n$ be the Fibonacci numbers. If $n\notin\{1,2,6,12\}$, then $F_n$ has a [primitive prime divisor](c:primitive-prime-divisor): a prime that divides $F_n$ and divides no $F_m$ with $0<m<n$.

hypotheses.text: The index $n$ is a positive integer different from $1,2,6,12$.

conclusion: Some prime divides $F_n$ and no earlier Fibonacci number.

proofs.name: Cyclotomic factors of Fibonacci numbers
proofs.slogan: Factor $F_n$ into cyclotomic parts and show that the last part is too large to hide only non-primitive primes.
proofs.scope: All $n$ outside the four exceptions; the exceptions $F_1=F_2=1$, $F_6=8$ and $F_{12}=144$ have no primitive prime.

roles.why: The bound on $|\Phi_n|$ holds for large $n$ and a finite check treats the small $n$.

steps.slogan: Factor $F_n$ as a product of integers $\Phi_d$ over the divisors $d$ of $n$.
steps.detail: With $\alpha,\beta=(1\pm\sqrt5)/2$, put $\Phi_d=\prod_{(k,d)=1}(\alpha-\zeta_d^k\beta)$. These are [cyclotomic polynomial](c:cyclotomic-polynomial)-type values and integers, and $F_n=\prod_{d\mid n}\Phi_d$.

steps.slogan: Show that primitive prime divisors of $F_n$ are the prime divisors of $\Phi_n$ that do not divide $n$.
steps.detail: A prime that divides $F_n$ and an earlier $F_m$ divides $F_{\gcd(n,m)}$, so it divides some $\Phi_d$ with $d<n$ a proper divisor. Such a prime divides $\Phi_n$ only if it divides $n$.

steps.slogan: Show that a non-primitive prime of $\Phi_n$ is the greatest prime factor of $n$.
steps.detail: A non-primitive prime $p$ of $\Phi_n$ has $n=p^am$ with $m$ the rank of $p$, and then $p$ divides $\Phi_n$ exactly once outside small cases. So $\Phi_n$ has no primitive prime only if $|\Phi_n|\le P(n)$, the greatest prime factor of $n$.

steps.slogan: Prove that $|\Phi_n|>n$ for large $n$ by estimating each factor.
steps.detail: Mobius inversion gives $\log|\Phi_n|=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(n/d)\log|\alpha^d-\beta^d|$ up to a constant. With $|F_d|\approx\alpha^d/\sqrt5$ this gives $\log|\Phi_n|\ge\varphi(n)\log\alpha-O(2^{\omega(n)})$, which exceeds $\log n$ for large $n$.

steps.slogan: Check the remaining small $n$ by computation.
steps.detail: Direct factorization of $F_n$ for the finitely many remaining $n$ shows that $F_n$ has a primitive prime exactly when $n\notin\{1,2,6,12\}$.

concepts.c:primitive-prime-divisor: The theorem asserts a primitive prime divisor and the proof separates it from non-primitive ones.
concepts.c:cyclotomic-polynomial: The factors $\Phi_d$ are values of cyclotomic-type polynomials.

source.ref: R. D. Carmichael, On the numerical factors of the arithmetic forms $\alpha^n\pm\beta^n$, Annals of Mathematics (2) 15 (1913), 30-48.
source.note: Carmichael proves the theorem for Lucas sequences, including the Fibonacci case; the outline follows his cyclotomic factorization.

statement: Let $\chi$ be a nontrivial [Dirichlet character](c:dirichlet-character) modulo an odd prime $p$ and $G(\chi)$ its [Gauss sum](c:gauss-sum). If $G(\chi)/\sqrt p$ is a [root of unity](c:root-of-unity), then $\chi$ is quadratic.

hypotheses.text: $\chi$ is a nontrivial Dirichlet character modulo an odd prime $p$.
The quotient $G(\chi)/\sqrt p$ is a root of unity.

proofs.name: Galois action on the Gauss sum
proofs.slogan: Use the Galois action on $G(\chi)^m$ and factorization of primes to rule out every order except 2.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem as an outline of the published proof; the converse, that quadratic Gauss sums are roots of unity times $\sqrt p$, is Gauss.

roles.why: The order $m$ of $\chi$ divides $p-1$, so $p$ is unramified in $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_m)$.
The root of unity condition makes $G(\chi)^m/p^{m/2}$ a root of unity.

steps.slogan: Show that $\sigma_a G(\chi)=\overline\chi(a)G(\chi)$ for the Galois element $\sigma_a$.
steps.detail: Take $\sigma_a$ with $\sigma_a(\zeta_p)=\zeta_p^a$ fixing $\zeta_m$. Substituting $x\mapsto ax$ in the sum gives the identity.

steps.slogan: Show that $G(\chi)^m$ lies in $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_m)$ and that $|G(\chi)|^2=p$.
steps.detail: The power $G^m$ is fixed by every $\sigma_a$, so it lies in $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_m)$. The identity $G\overline G=\chi(-1)p$ gives $|G|=\sqrt p$.

steps.slogan: Exclude odd order $m$ by ramification.
steps.detail: If $G=\varepsilon\sqrt p$ with $\varepsilon$ a root of unity and $m$ is odd, then $\varepsilon^m\sqrt p\in\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_m)$, because $p^{(m-1)/2}$ is rational. Then $p$ equals a unit times a square in a field where $p$ is unramified, which is impossible.

steps.slogan: Exclude even order $m>2$ by the prime factorization of Gauss sums.
steps.detail: Stickelberger-type formulas give the exponents of the primes above $p$ in $(G(\chi))^m$. They equal the exponents of $(p^{m/2})$ only when the order is 2.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $\chi$ has order 2.
steps.detail: Odd orders and even orders above 2 are excluded, and $\chi$ is nontrivial, so $m=2$.

concepts.c:dirichlet-character: The character is the object whose order the proof determines.
concepts.c:gauss-sum: The Gauss sum has fixed absolute value and a Galois action.
concepts.c:root-of-unity: The root of unity hypothesis forces a power of the sum to be a rational number times a unit.

source.ref: B. C. Berndt, R. J. Evans and K. S. Williams, Gauss and Jacobi Sums, Canadian Mathematical Society Series of Monographs and Advanced Texts, Wiley, 1998.
source.note: The book gives a proof of the Chowla-Mordell theorem; the original proofs are due independently to Chowla and Mordell around 1951.

statement: Let four lines in the plane be in general position: no two parallel and no three concurrent. The [circles](c:circle) through the vertices of the four triangles that three of the lines form all pass through one point.

hypotheses.text: The four lines have no two parallel and no three concurrent.

conclusion: The four circumcircles share a common point, the Clifford point of the four lines.

proofs.name: Miquel point and angle chase
proofs.slogan: Apply Miquel's theorem to three lines and the points of the fourth line, then show that the common point lies on the fourth circle.
proofs.scope: The first member of Clifford's chain; the next members (five lines, six lines, and so on) repeat the pattern with circles through a point.

roles.why: General position makes the six points $P_{ij}$ exist and keeps the triangles nondegenerate.

steps.slogan: Name the six intersection points and the four circles.
steps.detail: Let $P_{ij}$ be the meeting point of lines $\ell_i,\ell_j$, and $C_k$ the circle through the three points $P_{ij}$ with $i,j\ne k$. Then $P_{14},P_{24},P_{34}$ lie on $\ell_4$.

steps.slogan: Apply Miquel's theorem to the triangle of $\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3$.
steps.detail: The points $P_{14},P_{24},P_{34}$ lie on its sides $\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3$. The circles through each vertex and the two chosen points on its sides are $C_3$, $C_2$ and $C_1$, and Miquel's theorem gives a common point $M$.

steps.slogan: Compute the directed angle $\angle(MP_{12},MP_{13})$ by two of the circles.
steps.detail: On $C_3$ the angle $\angle(MP_{12},MP_{14})$ equals $\angle(\ell_2,\ell_4)$. On $C_2$ the angle $\angle(MP_{14},MP_{13})$ equals $\angle(\ell_4,\ell_3)$. Their sum is $\angle(\ell_2,\ell_3)$.

steps.slogan: Show that $M$ lies on the circle $C_4$ through $P_{12},P_{13},P_{23}$.
steps.detail: The vertex $P_{23}$ sees $P_{12},P_{13}$ at the directed angle $\angle(\ell_2,\ell_3)$, the same angle as $M$. So $M,P_{12},P_{13},P_{23}$ are concyclic.

concepts.c:circle: The four triangle circumcircles are the circles of the theorem.

source.note: The classical angle chase for the Wallace point of four lines; see H. S. M. Coxeter and S. L. Greitzer, Geometry Revisited, chapter 3, for Miquel's theorem.

statement: Let $\Gamma$ be a [discrete group](c:discrete-group) with left regular representation $\lambda$ and right regular representation $\rho$ on $\ell^2(\Gamma)$. For the [von Neumann algebra](c:von-neumann-algebra) $L(\Gamma)=\lambda(\Gamma)''$, the [commutant](c:commutant) is $L(\Gamma)'=\rho(\Gamma)''$.

hypotheses.text: $\Gamma$ is a discrete group acting on $\ell^2(\Gamma)$ by $\lambda$ and $\rho$.

conclusion: The commutant of $L(\Gamma)$ is the von Neumann algebra generated by the right regular representation.

proofs.name: Convolution operators commute
proofs.slogan: Describe operators commuting with left and right translations as convolutions, and show that they commute with each other.
proofs.scope: Any discrete group; the trace form of the theorem for the group algebra, with Murray and von Neumann's statement for a measure-preserving action as a sibling member.

roles.why: Discreteness gives the basis $\delta_g$ and the formulas of left and right translation.

steps.slogan: Show that $\rho(\Gamma)''\subseteq L(\Gamma)'$.
steps.detail: Right translation commutes with left translation, so $\rho(g)\in\lambda(\Gamma)'$. The commutant is a von Neumann algebra, so it contains $\rho(\Gamma)''$.

steps.slogan: Describe each $T\in L(\Gamma)'$ as right convolution by $\xi=T\delta_e$.
steps.detail: From $T\lambda_g=\lambda_gT$ we get $T\delta_g=\lambda_g\xi=\delta_g*\xi$. Thus $T\delta_g=\sum_h\xi(h)\delta_{gh}$, and $T$ is determined by $\xi\in\ell^2(\Gamma)$.

steps.slogan: Describe each $S\in\rho(\Gamma)'$ as left convolution by $\eta=S\delta_e$.
steps.detail: From $S\rho_g=\rho_gS$ we get $S\delta_g=\eta*\delta_g$. Thus $S\delta_g=\sum_k\eta(k)\delta_{kg}$, and $S$ is determined by $\eta\in\ell^2(\Gamma)$.

steps.slogan: Show that $S$ and $T$ commute.
steps.detail: For a basis vector, $ST\delta_g=S(\delta_g*\xi)$ and $TS\delta_g=T(\eta*\delta_g)$. Both equal the pointwise sum $\sum_{k,h}\eta(k)\xi(h)\delta_{kgh}$, absolutely convergent by Cauchy-Schwarz. By density and boundedness $ST=TS$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $\rho(\Gamma)'\subseteq L(\Gamma)$ and so $L(\Gamma)'=\rho(\Gamma)''$.
steps.detail: Every $S\in\rho(\Gamma)'$ commutes with $L(\Gamma)'=\lambda(\Gamma)'$, so $S\in\lambda(\Gamma)''=L(\Gamma)$. Taking commutants gives $L(\Gamma)'\subseteq\rho(\Gamma)''$, and step 1 gives the reverse inclusion.

concepts.c:discrete-group: Discreteness gives the standard basis of $\ell^2(\Gamma)$ and the translation formulas.
concepts.c:von-neumann-algebra: The algebra $L(\Gamma)$ is generated by the left translations.
concepts.c:commutant: The theorem identifies the commutant and the proof compares two commutants.

source.note: The standard argument of Murray and von Neumann for the group case, as in Kadison and Ringrose, Fundamentals of the Theory of Operator Algebras II, chapter 6.

statement: Let $X$ be a set and $F$ a family of partial functions $X\rightharpoonup\{0,1\}$ of [finite character](c:finite-character): a restriction of a member to a subset of its domain is a member, and a partial function belongs to $F$ when all its finite restrictions do. If every finite subset of $X$ is the domain of a member, then $F$ has a member with domain $X$.

hypotheses.text: A restriction of a member of $F$ to a subset of its domain belongs to $F$.
A partial function belongs to $F$ when all its finite restrictions belong to $F$.
Every finite subset of $X$ is the domain of some member of $F$.

proofs.name: Compactness of the Cantor cube
proofs.slogan: Make closed sets from the finite conditions in the compact space $\{0,1\}^X$ and intersect them.
proofs.scope: Any set $X$, including the empty set. The proof uses Tychonoff's theorem for $\{0,1\}^X$, which is equivalent to the Boolean prime ideal theorem and is weaker than the [axiom of choice](c:axiom-of-choice).

roles.why: Closure under restriction makes the sets $K_S$ decrease as $S$ grows.
Finite character turns membership of all finite restrictions into membership of the limit.
The finite domains make each set $K_S$ nonempty.

steps.slogan: Give $\{0,1\}^X$ the product topology and note that it is compact.
steps.detail: Each factor $\{0,1\}$ is a finite discrete space, so it is compact. Tychonoff's theorem then makes the product $\{0,1\}^X$ compact.

steps.slogan: Define the clopen sets $K_S$ of total functions whose restriction to $S$ lies in $F$.
steps.detail: For finite $S$ let $K_S=\{h:h|_S\in F\}$. The set depends on finitely many coordinates, so it is clopen. It is nonempty: take a member $f$ with domain $S$ and extend it by zeros.

steps.slogan: Show that the sets $K_S$ have the finite intersection property.
steps.detail: If $h\in K_{S\cup T}$, then $h|_S$ is a restriction of $h|_{S\cup T}\in F$, so $h\in K_S$. Thus $K_{S_1\cup\dots\cup S_n}\subseteq K_{S_1}\cap\dots\cap K_{S_n}$, and the intersection is nonempty.

steps.slogan: Take a point $h$ in all the sets $K_S$ by compactness.
steps.detail: The sets $K_S$ are closed with the finite intersection property in a compact space, so $\bigcap_S K_S\ne\emptyset$. Choose $h$ in it.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the total function $h$ belongs to $F$.
steps.detail: Every finite restriction $h|_S$ belongs to $F$ because $h\in K_S$. Finite character gives $h\in F$, and $h$ has domain $X$.

concepts.c:finite-character: Finite character lets the finite restrictions decide membership in $F$.
concepts.c:axiom-of-choice: The proof uses Tychonoff for the Cantor cube, weaker than choice.

source.note: The compactness argument for Engeler's lemma; see the discussion of prime ideal theorems and systems of finite character in the set-theoretic literature, for example the nLab entry for Engeler's lemma.
